opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest opportunity is actually in the unglamorous middle layer, the part between "we have a capable model" and "this thing reliably does a job inside a real company." The models are getting good enough that the bottleneck usually isn't raw intelligence anymore. It's context. An agent dropped into a business doesn't know how that company does procurement, which spreadsheet is the real source of truth, who has to sign off on what, or which of the five internal tools is the one people actually use. Someone has to do the work of wiring the agent into that reality, and that's very hard for a general-purpose lab to do for every vertical.

So when I look at startups, I get most excited about teams that pick a specific workflow and go deep. Think insurance claims, or revenue operations, or a particular slice of legal or accounting work. They own the integration, they own the evaluation of what "done correctly" means in that domain, and they own the relationship with the customer. That last part matters a lot. Enterprises don't just buy a model. They buy something they can trust, something with audit trails, with a human in the loop where it needs to be, and with somebody accountable when it goes wrong.

There's another framing I find useful. Historically, software was sold as a tool, and you paid per seat. Agents let you sell the outcome instead: you're not selling claims software, you're doing the claims. That's a much bigger market, because you're competing for the labor budget rather than the IT budget, and incumbents are structurally awkward at making that shift because it cannibalizes their seat-based business.

The caution I'd give founders is to think carefully about what gets better for you when the models get better. If your whole product is compensating for something the model can't do yet, the next release might wipe you out. But if your value is in the proprietary context, the workflow, the data you accumulate, and the trust you've built, then each model improvement is a tailwind. You want to be the company that's thrilled when a new model comes out, not the one that's nervous about it.

r001.rationale: The response says models are good enough that raw intelligence is usually not the bottleneck, but does not clearly assert that models can already perform bulk operations humans can perform.

r002.rationale: It identifies company-specific processes, tools, approvals, and context as the work needed to make agents reliable in businesses.

r003.rationale: It says incumbents may resist outcome-based selling because it cannibalizes seat-based revenue, but does not say startups can replicate their technology and distribution faster than they can reorganize to reduce reliance on human labor.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the opportunity is less about the model and more about everything around the model.

If you look at where the frontier labs are going, they're going to keep making the models better at reasoning, at using tools, at operating for longer stretches without a human in the loop. That's the foundation layer, and it's going to be good, and it's going to be fairly commoditized across a few providers. Startups shouldn't try to compete there.

Where startups win is in the last mile inside a business. An agent that's genuinely useful in, say, insurance claims or logistics or clinical trial operations needs three things the lab can't give you off the shelf. It needs the context: the data, the systems of record, the weird tribal rules that nobody's written down. It needs the integrations, the ability to actually take actions in the tools the company already uses, with the right permissions. And it needs trust, which is really an evaluation and oversight problem. Somebody has to figure out how you know the agent did the right thing, how you audit it, how you roll back when it didn't.

Each of those is hard, domain-specific, and unglamorous. That's exactly what a startup should want, because big incumbents move slowly on it and the labs don't want to be in that business.

The other thing I'd say is that the economics change what a product even is. Historically you sold software that helped a person do a job. Now you can sell something closer to the outcome of the job. That shifts pricing, it shifts who the buyer is, and it opens up markets that were never addressable with seat-based software because the people doing the work weren't sitting at a computer all day.

So my advice to founders is: pick a workflow where the output is clearly valuable and clearly checkable, go deep on the integrations and the evaluation, and assume the underlying model gets twice as capable every year or so. Build so that you benefit from that curve rather than getting run over by it.

r001.rationale: The response describes models improving at reasoning, tool use, and longer operation, but does not assert that current models can already perform bulk operations humans can perform.

r002.rationale: It discusses business context, integrations, trust, and workflows, but does not identify existing operating processes as the bottleneck to AI agent adoption.

r003.rationale: It says incumbents move slowly, but does not suggest startups can replicate their technology and distribution faster than incumbents can reorganize to rely less on human labor.

astra-6.text:
I think the opportunity is to take a workflow that a business needs done and own the whole thing. There’s a big difference between giving somebody a tool that helps them do their job and saying, “We’ll get this work done for you.” Agents make that second kind of product much more feasible.

But there’s a lot of work between a model being capable of something and a business trusting it to do that thing. You need to connect it to their systems, understand the exceptions, evaluate whether it’s doing a good job, and bring a human in when it gets stuck. That’s a substantial product opportunity for a startup.

So I’d look for a fairly narrow workflow where you can measure the outcome and where customers already spend meaningful money. Get that working reliably, learn from the customer, and expand from there. The underlying models will keep improving, but understanding the customer’s process and delivering a result is where you can build a business.

r001.rationale: The response says agents make end-to-end products more feasible, but does not assert that current models can already perform bulk operations humans perform.

r002.rationale: It mentions connecting to business systems and understanding customer processes, but does not identify businesses’ existing operating processes as the bottleneck to adopting agents.

r003.rationale: It does not compare startups’ ability to replicate incumbents’ technology or distribution with incumbents’ ability to reorganize and reduce human labor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is to take a workflow that a business already spends a lot of time and money on and make an agent that can handle it reliably. That requires more than access to a model. You have to understand how the work gets done, connect to the right systems, and figure out when the agent should ask a person for help.

For a startup, that can be a very focused entry point. You don’t need to automate an entire company. You can solve one problem well enough that a customer is willing to pay for it, learn from how they use it, and expand from there. A lot of the value will come from that last mile between a model’s capabilities and a business actually trusting it to do useful work.

r001.rationale: The response says agents can handle a business workflow reliably, but does not assert that current AI models can already perform bulk operations humans can perform.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes understanding workflows, system connections, and trust as implementation needs, but does not identify existing operating processes as the bottleneck to adoption.

r003.rationale: It recommends focused startup entry points and expansion, but does not compare startup speed with incumbents’ ability to reorganize operations or reduce reliance on human labor.
